question: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with integer side lengths and $AB<AC$. Points $D$ and $E$ lie on segments $BC$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $AD=AE=AB$. Line $DE$ intersects $AB$ at $X$. Circles $BXD$ and $CED$ intersect for the second time at $Y \neq D$. Suppose that $Y$ lies on line $AD$. There is a unique such triangle with minimal perimeter. This triangle has side lengths $a=BC$, $b=CA$, and $c=AB$. Find the remainder when $abc$ is divided by $10^{5}$.

A tournament is held with $2^{20}$ runners each of which has a different running speed. In each race, two runners compete against each other with the faster runner always winning the race. The competition consists of $20$ rounds with each runner starting with a score of $0$. In each round, the runners are paired in such a way that in each pair, both runners have the same score at the beginning of the round. The winner of each race in the $i^{\text{th}}$ round receives $2^{20-i}$ points and the loser gets no points.

At the end of the tournament, we rank the competitors according to their scores. Let $N$ denote the number of possible orderings of the competitors at the end of the tournament. Let $k$ be the largest positive integer such that $10^k$ divides $N$. What is the remainder when $k$ is divided by $10^{5}$?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB \neq AC$, circumcircle $\Omega$, and incircle $\omega$. Let the contact points of $\omega$ with $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ be $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Let the circumcircle of $AFE$ meet $\Omega$ at $K$ and let the reflection of $K$ in $EF$ be $K'$. Let $N$ denote the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $EF$. The circle tangent to line $BN$ and passing through $B$ and $K$ intersects $BC$ again at $T \neq B$. 
    
Let sequence $(F_n)_{n \geq 0}$ be defined by $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and for $n \geq 2$, $F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$. Call $ABC$ $n$\emph{-tastic} if $BD = F_n$, $CD = F_{n+1}$, and $KNK'B$ is cyclic. Across all $n$-tastic triangles, let $a_n$ denote the maximum possible value of $\frac{CT \cdot NB}{BT \cdot NE}$. Let $\alpha$ denote the smallest real number such that for all sufficiently large $n$, $a_{2n} < \alpha$. Given that $\alpha = p + \sqrt{q}$ for rationals $p$ and $q$, what is the remainder when $\left\lfloor p^{q^p} \right\rfloor$ is divided by $99991$?

Alice and Bob are each holding some integer number of sweets. Alice says to Bob: ``If we each added the number of sweets we're holding to our (positive integer) age, my answer would be double yours. If we took the product, then my answer would be four times yours.'' Bob replies: ``Why don't you give me five of your sweets because then both our sum and product would be equal.'' What is the product of Alice and Bob's ages?

A $500 \times 500$ square is divided into $k$ rectangles, each having integer side lengths. Given that no two of these rectangles have the same perimeter, the largest possible value of $k$ is $\mathcal{K}$. What is the remainder when $k$ is divided by $10^{5}$?

A rectangular prism of dimensions $41 \times 51 \times 61$ is partitioned into $41 \times 51 \times 61$ unit cubes. Each unit cube is colored either red or blue. It is known that every $2 \times 2 \times 2$ block of 8 unit cubes within the prism contains at most 4 red unit cubes. What is the maximum possible number of red unit cubes in the entire prism?

The integers from 1 to 137043, inclusive, are written on a whiteboard in a single row in some arbitrary order. For every pair of adjacent numbers in this row, their greatest common divisor (GCD) is calculated and written on a separate piece of paper. What is the maximum possible number of distinct integers that can be found on the piece of paper?

Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function. A "chord" of the function $f$ is defined as a line segment of integer length that is parallel to the x-axis, such that both of its endpoints lie exactly on the graph of $f$. Suppose it is known that the graph of $f$ has exactly $N$ such chords, and one of these chords has a length of 36501. Find the minimum possible value of $N$.

A city plaza is represented as a $12 \times 12$ square grid of cells. On New Year's Eve, it suddenly starts snowing, and from then on, exactly $5$ cm of snow falls on each cell every night (snow only falls at night). Every morning, a janitor chooses exactly one row or one column of the grid and sweeps all the snow from it onto an adjacent row or column. This means the snow from each cell in the chosen row or column is moved to the corresponding neighboring cell in the adjacent row or column. Sweeping snow outside the boundaries of the plaza is strictly forbidden. On the evening of the 133rd day of the year (after exactly 133 nights of snowfall and 133 mornings of sweeping), an inspector arrives at the plaza and measures the height of the snow in the cell that has the highest snowdrift. The janitor's goal is to plan his daily sweeps such that the height of this maximum snowdrift is minimized. Assuming the janitor acts optimally to achieve this goal, what is the height (in cm) of the highest snowdrift the inspector will find?

There are 130 cities in a country, and initially there are no roads. The government randomly determines the cost of building a two-way road between every pair of cities. The costs are assigned such that each of the $\frac{130 \times 129}{2}$ possible roads receives a distinct integer cost from 1 to $\frac{130 \times 129}{2}$, with all permutations of costs being equally likely. The mayor of each city selects the single cheapest road among the 129 possible roads connecting their city to others, and this road is built (if two mayors select the same road, it is built only once). After these roads are built, the cities are partitioned into $M$ connected components (cities in the same component can reach each other via built roads, while cities in different components cannot). The expected value of $M$ can be expressed as an irreducible fraction $\frac{P}{Q}$, where $P$ and $Q$ are coprime positive integers. What is the value of $P + Q$?

In each row of a $50 \times n$ table, the integers from $1$ to $50$ are written in some order such that no numbers are repeated in any row (the table has $n$ rows and $50$ columns). It is allowed to swap two numbers within the same row if they differ by exactly $1$, provided they are not adjacent to each other. It is known that no two rows in the table can be made identical using any sequence of such operations. Let $N$ be the greatest possible value of $n$ for which this is possible. What is the remainder when $N$ is divided by $100000$?

There are $25000$ points marked on a plane, no three of which are collinear. Vasily draws all line segments connecting pairs of marked points, one by one. At each step, when drawing the next segment $S$, Vasily labels it with the smallest positive integer that has not yet been used to label any segment sharing a common endpoint with $S$. What is the largest positive integer $k$ such that Vasily can choose the order of drawing the segments to eventually label some segment with the number $k$?

Sasha claims that for any set of $43211$ rays in space, no two of which intersect, he can always choose $k$ distinct points on the union of these rays such that all $k$ points lie on the surface of the same sphere. The chosen points are not required to lie on distinct rays; multiple chosen points may lie on the same ray. What is the maximum value of $k$ for which his claim is guaranteed to be true?

For some positive integers $n$ and $m$ with $n > m$, the number $n$ can be represented as the sum of $74321$ terms, each of which is a non-negative integer power of $m$. The same number $n$ can also be represented as the sum of $21054$ terms, each of which is a non-negative integer power of $m+1$. What is the maximum possible value of $m$ for which this could happen (for at least one such $n$)?

In a certain alphabet, there are exactly three letters: $X$, $Y$, and $Z$. A "word" is defined as a sequence of $50$ letters that contains exactly $16$ letters from the set $\{X, Y\}$ and exactly $34$ letters $Z$. What is the maximum possible number of words that can be chosen such that for any two chosen words, there is at least one corresponding position where both words have a letter from the set $\{X, Y\}$, but these letters are different? (i.e., in that position, one word has $X$ and the other has $Y$).
